teaching.causalExplanation: Group A did blocked practice: one skill repeated many times before the next. Group B did random practice: several skills mixed in an unpredictable order. In blocked practice, each hit is a small tweak of the last, so it looks smooth. In random practice, the other strokes push the plan out of mind, so on every hit she rebuilds it from scratch. That rebuilding is hard work, makes each hit worse, and is exactly what a match demands. So we need two words. Performance is how well you do it right now. Learning is a lasting change, and you only see it later, in a retention test after a delay. A coach at training sees performance, and hopes for learning. Here they moved in opposite directions. One catch: a beginner has no plan to rebuild yet. So block to acquire, then shuffle to retain. Two more choices have clear rules. Massed practice has little rest. Distributed practice has real rest between attempts or sessions. A beginner usually needs distributed practice, because the movement uses all her attention, and a tired beginner practises errors. Practice doesn't make perfect, it makes permanent. Massed practice suits short, easy skills and experienced learners. Whole practice does the full skill, and part practice splits it. The scale from last time decides. A continuous skill is mostly taught as a whole, with drills like kick and pull as practice parts. A serial skill can be split, then joined two parts at a time, then done whole. The syllabus also names performance elements, the parts of an open skill that aren't the movement. Decision-making is choosing the right response, under time pressure, with incomplete information. A drill with one right answer can't train it. Small-sided games and drills with two real options can. A coach calling out a shuffled order isn't a decision, either. The player has to choose from what she reads. Strategy is the plan made before a contest, like pressing high. Tactics are changes made during it, like whether to keep pressing when you're two goals down. Strategy is planned by studying the opposition, then rehearsed in training. Tactics grow from game situations and questions. Before, or during: that's the difference.

- **Reuse:** v16's `StageTrack` (7); v17's `SkillContinua` (opening, and small in 3 and 4).

Labelled "illustrative pattern"; the finding's source is v19's job.

- **Open decisions for root.** (1) Site correction 24. No new plates.

Handoff: researching skill acquisition (route entry hms-y11-m2-v19). **Handoff frame (hms-y11-m2-v19 opens from it):** the `RetentionCurves` centred (blocked teal, random orange, crossing at the retention test), with an empty citation tag hanging from the crossing point reading "source: ?" and a grey label "where did this finding come from?"; the "Next" chip at the lower right reads "Next: how do you check what the evidence says?"; this video's heading at the top left.

scenes.teachingReason: Group A did blocked practice: one skill repeated many times before the next. Group B did random practice: several skills mixed in an unpredictable order. In blocked practice, each hit is a small tweak of the last, so it looks smooth. In random practice, the other strokes push the plan out of mind, so on every hit she rebuilds it from scratch. That rebuilding is hard work, makes each hit worse, and is exactly what a match demands. So we need two words. Performance is how well you do it right now. Learning is a lasting change, and you only see it later, in a retention test after a delay. A coach at training sees performance, and hopes for learning. Here they moved in opposite directions. One catch: a beginner has no plan to rebuild yet. So block to acquire, then shuffle to retain.

Tactics grow from game situations and questions. Before, or during: that's the difference.

scenes.teachingReason: The syllabus names six types of feedback, but they're really three questions, and every comment answers all three. Where did it come from? Task-intrinsic feedback comes from doing the skill: what you feel, see and hear. Augmented feedback is added from outside, by a coach, a video or a timing gate. When did it arrive? Concurrent feedback comes during the movement, and delayed feedback after it. Concurrent feedback only helps when the movement is slow enough to act on, like a long swim, not a half-second shot. And what is it about? Knowledge of results is the outcome: it went wide. Knowledge of performance is the movement that caused it: your shoulders opened early. A player who's just missed already knows the result. What she needs is the reason.
scenes.narrationCue: Task-intrinsic / Augmented / Concurrent / delayed / Knowledge of results / Knowledge of performance
